To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
rectal bleeding has a poor sensitivity and a poor positive predictive value for rectal and/or sigmoid polyps or adenomas.
rectal bleeding has a low sensitivity (33%) and low positive predictive value (8%) for detecting rectal or sigmoid adenomas.
rectal bleeding in apparently healthy subjects is a relatively common symptom but does not identify a large number of patients who have colorectal polyps.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an integrated model for the analysis and prediction of human behavior in complex, uncertain and dynamic environments.
the relationship between rectal bleeding and colorectal cancer.
the development of a new generation of high-resolution, high-frequency ultrasound probes and their use in clinical practice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

in a screening program for colorectal polyps and cancer, the presence of overt rectal bleeding in an otherwise asymptomatic person is a relatively insensitive, specific, and non-diagnostic sign of the presence of a polyp or cancer in the lower gastrointestinal tract.
the predictive value of overt rectal bleeding in a healthy population is low and that sigmoidoscopy in such subjects is unlikely to detect appreciable numbers of polyps or cancers.
rectal bleeding in the general population is not a good screening test for rectal and/or sigmoid polyps or colorectal cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
rectal bleeding is not an effective screening test for rectal or distal sigmoid polyps and cancer.
rectal bleeding is not an effective method of selecting apparently healthy men over 50 for flexible sigmoidoscopy.
the predictive value for rectal and/or sigmoid polyps and cancer of rectal bleeding was low, and that this was not influenced by regular stool inspection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
if you have rectal bleeding, you should not delay getting it checked out, but it is also important to remember that rectal bleeding is common and is often not caused by polyps or cancer.
if you have rectal bleeding, don’t panic.
rectal bleeding is not a good predictor of polyp presence.
